transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herbst.
With just two weeks until Election Day,
the map of competitive House and Senate races
is expanding deeper into conservative territory.
President Trump is campaigning this week
in perennial purple and deep red states,
today's in North Carolina, tomorrow in South Carolina.
And here's Stephen Fowler says Republicans have put
a lot of money into this year's races.
Over the last three weeks, data shows Republicans
have doubled, tripled, even quadrupled their investment
in places like the Senate race in Kansas and Mississippi,
red House districts in Missouri, Pennsylvania, Kentucky.
And they've pulled back from the Georgia, North Carolina
Senate races and one-time toss-up races in Iowa,
Ohio and Nebraska that are not as competitive anymore.
And here's Stephen Fowler.
And President Trump says he's already spent $300 million
so far and plans to spend another $100 million.
Meanwhile, the billionaire and former New York City mayor
Mike Bloomberg today pledged $80 million to help Democrats.
President Trump boasted this weekend of his growing power
in his second term.
And here's Franco Ordonez has more on Trump's willingness
to act unilaterally and how he's using the executive power
to make his case to midterm voters.
Less than three weeks before the election,
Trump continues to crash through barriers
that he wouldn't dare cross in his first term.
His Justice Department is raiding a Congresswoman's home,
he's going after the press, and he's making deals with Russia
that fly in the face of congressionally passed sanctions.
Tevi Troy, a presidential historian, says Trump
is not the first president to test the limits
of his executive authority, but he says Trump
is using the power to get around congressional gridlock
and going after political and cultural opponents.
And that's the way he's really run his second term,
is what I call a unilateralist.
He doesn't have an ideology, he has a methodology.
And he says that methodology is unilateralism.
Franco Ordonez, NPR News.
General Motors says profits were up compared to last year
in his third quarter earnings report,
but electric vehicle sales were down.
NPR's Willa Rubin has more.
Just over a year ago, a $7,500 federal tax credit
that helped people buy and lease electric vehicles went away.
In an earnings call with analysts, GM executives said
that helps explain why its EV sales fell in the past year.
Data from Edmunds and Cox Automotive shows
that's been true industry-wide.
But GM says it's continuing to make EVs.
Executives say GM is "right-sizing its capacity
to align EV production with demand,"
and EV sales are growing abroad.
In Europe last year, over 30% of new cars sold were electric.
In China, more than half were.
That's according to the International Energy Agency.
In the meantime, GM's gas-powered trucks helped make up for its losses.
Willa Rubin, NPR News.
Just before the close, Wall Street was in mixed territory.
You're listening to NPR News.
New research shows the demand for technology
to power artificial intelligence is on track to outpace development.
NPR's Kristen Wright reports.
Research by Goldman Sachs says the development of data centers
is happening at a much slower pace than the speed of the AI race.
The investment firm expects global demand for power to support AI
to rise 170% by 2030,
creating bottlenecks of projects awaiting approval and grid connections.
The report calls for a new playbook and capital solutions
to address the data center strain on local power grids
and concerns over rising electricity bills.
Many communities oppose the building of data centers
and their neighborhoods.
Some states have temporary bans,
while others are considering pauses on construction.
Goldman projects Big Tech will borrow $420 billion next year
to finance AI infrastructure and development.
Kristen Wright, NPR News, Washington.
The Supreme Court has agreed to hear a case about a federal ban
on distilling liquor at home.
The case centers on an 1868 law banning the practice
because Congress wanted to protect tax revenue.
And the Trump administration supports the law,
saying billions of dollars is at risk.
Iron mortgage rates are hitting the housing market hard.
The Commerce Department says housing starts
and building permits in September fell more sharply
than economists were predicting, down 5.2%.
And according to the National Association of Realtors Pending Home Sales,
a measure of signed contracts on existing homes
dropped 7.3% in September from the month before
and were down 11.3% year over year.
I'm Janene Herbst, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Trump campaigns in North Carolina and South Carolina as midterm races expand into conservative territory
Republicans shift midterm spending toward Kansas, Mississippi, Missouri, Pennsylvania and Kentucky races
Mike Bloomberg pledges $80 million to help Democrats in the midterm elections
Franco Ordonez reports on Trump's unilateral use of executive power, including a Justice Department raid on a congresswoman's home
General Motors reports higher third-quarter profits but falling electric vehicle sales after the federal EV tax credit ended
Goldman Sachs report warns AI power demand will outpace data center development and strain power grids
Supreme Court agrees to hear case on federal ban on distilling liquor at home
US housing starts and building permits fall sharply in September, and pending home sales drop 7.3%
